Father,

As I was preparing for my journey last night, I attempted to find a certain lute of mine which was the favorite among my collection. It has gone missing from its case. I'm certain Hamlet stole it. If you could somehow arrange its return during my absence, I would be overjoyed. Please don't hesitate to get Bernardo involved.

All my love, Laertes

I am Elise, lady to the Queen, servant all my life. They say I am mad with fever. But this is truth. Hear my final story, if you are able, if you care a whit, if you can know its significance.

I was barely more than a child myself when Simona was first let into the castle, a glowing vision of a girl dressed in a peasant's rags. Even then the head scullery maid ordered her hair be covered so she didn't attract 'attention'. In the end, it made no difference.

Simona was kind to me. This, I recall. I often helped the girl with her work as she braided the Queen's hair. After she was finished, Queen Astrid would beg her to stay, to tell stories. Simona had a way with stories. She never refused. And when King Alexander came to bed and woo Simona, who was she to refuse him, either?

Then there was the book. That horrid book... Simona brought it home. From where? Who gave it to her? I still don't know. Four days later, news of Queen Astrid's sudden death shocked the castle into mute horror, and Simona was quietly whisked away to the King's chambers. She was now the King's only lover. A low-born nobody with the power to rule nations.

The guards whispered of Queen Astrid's body: of how she died with her own nails lodged in her throat, the flesh torn, gone abruptly and thoroughly mad, her blood seeping through the keep tower's floor.

Simona came to me early one morning when it was still dark, inconsolably upset and without a light. "The book is cursed," She whispered to me in the darkness, her face wet with tears. "Elise, you don't understand. I was trapped in Elsinore for ever, for a thousand years or more. I saw every outcome I could, every possible version of this world, and it was all rotten. What could I do, Elise? What could I do? The book made me choose, and I chose to let Astrid rot with it all, so I could rule..."

She kissed me goodbye and pressed a coin into my hand. "I cannot hide from God," she said. "But I cannot stay in Elsinore. Tell no one where I went. Promise me, Elise."

And here I am, breaking that promise. I know Simona lives. What happened that insane week all those years ago? What will become of little Ophelia and Laertes, and my beloved husband I left behind? I will go to my grave not knowing.

Should my family ever read this, know this: I lived a far luckier life than any woman of my station ought to have enjoyed. But the luckiest thing in my world was always you.

我是伊莉丝，王后的侍女，一辈子都在服侍人。他们说我发烧烧疯了。但这些都是真的。请听听我最后的故事，只要你还能听，只要你还有一点在乎，只要你能明白它意味着什么。

西蒙娜初次获准进入城堡时，我自己也才刚过孩童的年纪。她穿着农家人的破衣烂衫，却美得光彩照人。那时，洗碗女仆的领班就命令她把头发遮起来，免得引来“注意”。到头来，这也没起什么作用。

西蒙娜待我很好。这一点，我记得。她为王后编头发时，我常常帮她做事。编完之后，阿斯特丽德王后总会央求她留下来讲故事。西蒙娜很会讲故事。她从不拒绝。而当亚历山大国王来向西蒙娜求欢、与她同床时，她又哪有资格拒绝他呢？

后来，那本书出现了。那本可怕的书……西蒙娜把它带回了家。从哪里来的？是谁给她的？我至今都不知道。四天后，阿斯特丽德王后猝死的消息让整个城堡陷入惊恐，鸦雀无声，而西蒙娜被悄悄带进了国王的寝宫。如今，她成了国王唯一的情人。一个出身卑微的无名之辈，却有了统治列国的权力。

卫兵们悄声议论着阿斯特丽德王后的尸体：她死时，自己的指甲还扎在喉咙里，皮肉被撕破；她突然彻底疯了，鲜血渗过了主堡塔楼的地板。

一天清晨，天还没亮，西蒙娜就来找我。她悲痛欲绝，也没带灯。“那本书受了诅咒，”她在黑暗中低声对我说，满脸都是泪。“伊莉丝，你不明白。我被永远困在埃尔西诺，困了一千年，甚至更久。我看遍了我能看到的每一种结局，这个世界每一种可能的模样，全都腐烂不堪。我能怎么办，伊莉丝？我能怎么办？那本书逼我选择，而我选择让阿斯特丽德和这一切一起腐烂，好让我掌权……”

她吻了我，向我道别，又把一枚钱币塞进我手里。“我躲不过上帝，”她说，“但我不能留在埃尔西诺。别告诉任何人我去了哪里。答应我，伊莉丝。”

而现在，我却在违背那个承诺。我知道西蒙娜还活着。多年前那个疯狂的星期里，究竟发生了什么？年幼的奥菲莉娅和雷欧提斯，还有我留下的心爱丈夫，往后会怎样？我到死都不会知道。

如果我的家人有一天读到这些，请记住：我这一生的幸运，远远超过了像我这样身份的女人所能奢望的。但在我的世界里，最幸运的事，始终是有你们。

Again... again... again... Polonius, not even you can save your master from Hell this time.

I concede defeat on ever finding that book. The Hand of Dionysus, they call it. I find references, mentions, breadcrumbs. Did you know it's been mentioned as far back as Judas Iscariot, and even older still? Polonius, find the book so that no one must suffer, must die like this.

Time is nothing. Death is nothing. For the last hundred years alone I have lain in the garden, awaiting the trickle of my brother's poison in my ear a thousand times. Again and again and again. How cruel should it be that this gap of time seems to begin and end with me lying in the garden on a warm spring morning? How does my brother always find a way to kill me? Is his hatred of me truly so strong? And my wife—my wife, her faithfulness useless, meaningless, the bridal bed soiled with another's lust...

Let her have him if she loves him so much. Let them cavort in the halls of Elsinore, and some year hence, the chambers of Hell. I could not say goodbye to my only son. My regrets burn in my throat like acid, like poison. I can say goodbye only to you.

So farewell, my faithful advisor. Bury me far from Claudius if it's the last thing you do. I can hear the playmaster's foosteps in the hallway, here to relieve me from this endless madness. I give up. I give up.

又一次……又一次……又一次……波洛涅斯，这一次，连你也救不了你的主人，让他免下地狱。

要找到那本书，我认输了。他们称它为“狄俄尼索斯之手”。我找到了一些记载、提及它的文字、零星的线索。你知道吗，早在加略人犹大的时代，就有人提到过它，甚至还要更早？波洛涅斯，找到那本书，让所有人都不必再这样受苦、这样死去。

时间算不了什么。死亡算不了什么。仅仅过去这一百年，我就已在花园里躺过一千次，等着弟弟的毒药滴进我的耳朵。一次又一次，一次又一次。这段时间竟以我在温暖的春日清晨躺在花园里为起点，又以此为终点，这该是何等残酷？为什么弟弟总能找到杀我的办法？他对我的恨，当真如此深吗？还有我的妻子——我的妻子，她的忠贞毫无用处，毫无意义，新婚的床榻被另一个人的欲望玷污……

她既然那么爱他，就让她得到他吧。让他们在埃尔西诺的厅堂里尽情嬉闹，再过些年，就去地狱的房间里继续。我没能向我唯一的儿子道别。悔恨灼烧着我的喉咙，像酸液，像毒药。我只能向你道别。

那么，永别了，我忠诚的顾问。哪怕这是你最后能做的一件事，也要把我葬在远离克劳狄斯的地方。我听见了戏剧大师在走廊里的脚步声，他来让我摆脱这无尽的疯狂了。我放弃了。我放弃了。

entries.source: June 6, MDXXXV Ophelia will not even look at me. My love for her means nothing now. And in the great hall, they rejoice my uncle's crowning, my father's proud form but a distant memory. If my uncle does not allow me to return to Wittenberg soon, I fear I will well and truly perish. August 8 That thing was not my father. It can't be. My father lies buried. But if it wasn't my father... what devil or evil spirit was it? Am I truly losing my mind? Was it real? Can I be certain it wasn't just a horrid dream? No, the others saw it too... even if they won't speak to me of it. My uncle cannot be trusted. Devils disregarded, there is yet something evil in him. I found the literature which Bernardo mentioned, tucked away in the gallery downstairs... it only confirms my suspicions. And yet... something in me keeps me from acting on it. What has stolen my courage?

My glass shall not persuade me I am old
So long as youth and thou are one of date.
But when in thee time's furrows I behold,
Then look I death my days should expiate.
For all that beauty that doth cover thee
Is but the seemingly raiment of my heart
Which in thy breast doth live, as thine in mine.
How can I then be elder than thou art?
O therefore, love, be of thyself so wary
As I, not for myself, but for thee will,
Bearing thy heart, which I will keep so chary
As tender nurse her babe from faring ill.
Presume not on thy heart when mine is slain;
Thou gav'st me thine not to give back again.

只要青春与你同龄，
镜子便休想劝我承认衰老。
可当我见时光在你脸上犁出沟痕，
便盼死亡为我的岁月作了结。
因为覆在你身上的一切美丽，
不过是我心披在外面的衣裳；
我的心住在你胸中，如你的心住在我胸中。
如此，我又怎会比你年长？
所以，爱人啊，请珍重你自己，
如我也会珍重自己，不为我，而为你；
我怀着你的心，必将悉心守护，
如温柔的乳母护着婴孩，免遭伤害。
若我的心已死，莫以为你的心仍可安然；
你将它给了我，便不是要我再归还。

My Dearest Gertrude,

I hope this letter finds you in excellent health. Although I have not had the pleasure of your company in some years, I hope you will remember me fondly, Aunt, as I do you. I write to you with news of your sister, my most beloved Aunt Margaret.

Not one month ago, as one of her maids served a meal, the maid happened to drop a glass goblet, causing it to shatter. One of those shattered fragments entered Margaret's foot, and caused her to take gravely ill as the wound festered. Her physician recommended the limb be removed, and Margaret, then in good health, bade it be so. Yet on the very morning she was to undergo such a thing, she passed into the arms of God. You will be pleased to hear, I am certain, that the sacrament was administered in advance. May God rest her eternal soul.

I know that Margaret would have wanted you by her side in her final moments. Take comfort in the fact that she loved you dearly, and spoke of you often in her last few days.

Your faithful nephew,
Charles

我最亲爱的乔特鲁德：

愿您收到这封信时身体康健。虽然已有数年未能有幸与您相聚，我仍希望，姨母，您能像我思念您一样，怀着温情记起我。我写信是要告诉您关于您姐妹的消息，她也是我最亲爱的玛格丽特姨母。

Have you often wondered at the true form and character of your lover? Pay careful mind: here are eight signs he's foe rather than friend! 

FIRST, within mere days of your acquaintance, he declares that if you 'call him but love, he'll be new baptis'd.' This nobleman is a walking source of dramatic show, clinging to any poor girl who crosses his path. Abnormally likely to meet his end in poison and tears.

SECOND, he uses the term 'taming' or 'shrew' in your presence—or even worse, in the same sentence. If he attempts to starve you to break your will, eat his heart out.

THIRD, he suddenly finds himself madly in love with your closest friend after promising you his undying heart. Keep a sharp eye out for faerie dust in the vicinity. 

FOURTH, he sticks a dagger in your back, then blames it on your 'ambition.' Don't worry: your restless spirit will have revenge. Stay indoors on March 15 if possible.

FIVE, after you help him murder his friends and cover up the crimes, he begins embarrassing you with inappropriate sobbing at your dinner parties. Even the most heartening prophecy can't revive this relationship. 

SIX, he tells you your wife has been unfaithful, but offers flimsy proof. Take a walk, enjoy some deep breathing, and stay away from pillows.

SEVEN, he tries to convince you to kill your brother. One might think this clear as day, yet this author is continually surprised.

EIGHT, sometimes he tells you to get to a nunnery. Other times he tells you he 'did love you once.' Which is it? Send this uncouth boy sulking back to university!

你是否常常琢磨，恋人的真面目和品性究竟如何？请留个心眼：下面八个征兆，说明他是敌人，而非朋友！ 

第一，才认识几天，他就宣称，只要你“叫他一声爱人，他便重新受洗”。这位贵族浑身都是戏，见到哪个可怜姑娘都要纠缠一番。他死于毒药与泪水的可能性高得离谱。

第二，他当着你的面说起“驯服”或“悍妇”——更糟的是，把这两个词用在同一句话里。他若想靠饿着你来磨掉你的意志，那就把他的心挖出来吃掉。

第三，刚向你许下永不变心的誓言，他就突然疯狂地爱上了你最亲密的朋友。留意一下附近有没有仙子的魔法粉。 

第四，他在你背后捅了一刀，却说都是你的“野心”惹的祸。别担心：你不得安息的亡魂自会报仇。三月十五日，能不出门就别出门。

第五，你帮他杀害朋友、掩盖罪行之后，他却在你的晚宴上哭哭啼啼，失态得让你难堪。再鼓舞人心的预言，也救不了这段关系。 

第六，他说你的妻子对你不忠，却拿不出像样的证据。出去散散步，做几个深呼吸，别碰枕头。

第七，他试图说服你杀死自己的兄弟。这迹象似乎再明显不过了，可笔者仍一再为此感到惊讶。

第八，他一会儿叫你进修道院，一会儿又说他“曾经确实爱过你”。到底哪句才算数？把这个没教养的小子赶回大学，让他自己生闷气去！

entries.source: MARCH This morning I awoke from a vision of God as I slept. I saw Him before me in all His glory, and He spoke to me. When the dream faded, I realized my face was wet with tears. The Lord told me to enter the service of a certain Duke Iocus living in a town near here, and to oversee the man's baptism. This particular Duke was orphaned as a child, and as such, his holy education had been sorely neglected. I knew I had no choice but to obey God's will and to go seek out this man. That very dawn, I packed my things, paid the tab at my inn, and traveled over field and hill until I reached the gates of Duke Iocus's estate. Duke Iocus is a man of notorious reputation, to be certain; handsome, but wicked. Of course, as I have sworn a vow of modesty and chastity, I knew his wicked vices would have no influence on me. I knocked once and, hearing a shout, interpreted it as an invitation to enter. Imagine my surprise when I found the good Duke himself in the middle of beastly fornication with a young maiden... on the floor of the foyer, no less. The two of them were braying and sweating as nothing I'd ever seen. Flushing red, I coughed politely to make my presence known, but the Duke merely rolled over and lazily extended a hand in greeting. "Ahh, a cleric!" He boomed. "What brings you to my estate?" I introduced myself and declared my purpose to him, asking if he wished to be baptised. He roared with laughter. "What rubbish!" He explained to me that he had no need for a holy man, but all the need in the world for a stalwart butler... and so, before I could think of anything better, I agreed to serve him in that capacity. "I warn you, my new cleric butler," Iocus swore, "I shall never believe in any God you serve." He may say this now, but I believe I can change his heart. APRIL My lord Iocus has kept me busy this last month. One of my continual duties is to ensure the sanctity of his personal bedchamber, especially its cleanliness, so that he might continue to seduce all manner of impressionable young folk into it at all hours of the day and night. His lust seems to know no boundaries. I find it both frightening and some matter of clinical interest to me. Today, when tidying his chamber, I thought I might leave my bible at his bedside. Surely, I thought, he might read a page or two? I was right. He pushed into my room later that evening without knocking and handed the bible back to me. "What a fascinating book!" he declared. "Have you come to know God?" "Sort of. I read only the book called Song of Songs. I learned so many fascinating ways to compliment a woman's breasts. Never read anything so erotic in my life!" "And what of the rest of it, my liege?" He shrugged. "Dull. Dry. Lacking in action, heavy-handed on miracles to service the plot. Couldn't get through half of it without falling asleep." He spun on his heel and left. MAY For the last month, my lord Iocus kindly allowed me to bring a prayer group into his home. It is but once a week, on the sabbath. Tonight's subject was on preparing oneself to enter the communion of marriage and opening one's heart to God. Three young women and three young men came to our door, all of them in their finest clothing, ready to receive the Word. Ordinarily Iocus is prone to leaving home on nights like these to drink and play, but tonight he seemed compelled to linger. Not one hour in, after the wine had been served, Iocus came to me. "We've nothing to serve them to eat!" he fretted. "Nothing but bread and cheese. What sort of a meal is that? My good cleric, run into town and purchase an entire boar at once!" I donned my cloak, took a satchel of gold, and started off, giving the group my apologies. ...But three hours later, I returned to a scene which disturbed me to my core. Around the threshold of the front door were strewn half a dozen empty wineskins. Entering the foyer, I saw two of the young women giggling and chasing after the lads—all of them naked as babes and red in the face. From upstairs, I could faintly hear the sound of distant moans. "My Duke!" I called out. "What manner of sin is going on in this home?" Six voices rang out in muffled, sensual laughter. "What manner, indeed. I can be as specific as you like!" Duke Iocus called back, the seventh voice, barely stifling his own laugh. "Though we're, ah, preoccupied. Friends, make room in the bath—I'm coming in!" I think I must have gone into a dead faint, then. I knelt on the floor and prayed with all my might. Later that night, Iocus burst into my chambers. His hair was wild, his eyes rolling. He was stark naked. "Praise God!" He shouted. "I beg your pardon?" I said, bleary and half-awake. "My dear cleric, I've seen the light! I want you to baptise me immediately. Tomorrow at dawn, if possible!" "My lord," I said in shock, "What changed your mind?" Iocus shook his head. "I was nestled in a pile of limbs and lovemaking for hours. I thought for a moment I might die entwined like that. And I did experience a death, of sorts. But then, at the moment of release, a sense of utter peace came over me, the manner of which I can hardly describe. I've never felt so content! So magical! So right! I remembered all your endlessly dull lectures about the Holy Spirit. And I knew then that surely this must be your God's way of speaking through me. This must be how you feel every day!" I stared for a moment in horror. Neither of us spoke. "...So you'll be baptised?" I ventured after a long silence. "Right away, my good man. I want to be a Christian!" "Fair enough," I said, and went back to sleep. The Lord works in mysterious ways.

Hear me, young maidens who have traveled wild,
Whose eyes have never seen the touch of death,
Who tarry often when the sun grows dim,
Who linger long by cairns and caverns dark.

I once was you in spirit and in heart.
I am Persephone, the taken one.
When I was young I planted seeds alone,
And gathered flowers freely in the sun.

One day the earth burst forth with violent seams
And ashes belched with spite upon the land.
King Hades, Lord of Death, had come for me,
To seize and make me his unwilling bride.

At first I cried out to the world above,
But no one heard the call to grab my hand.
He pulled me down into the low beyond,
And I knew this was where I'd make my grave.

No flowers grew within the world of death.
I fell upon the ground and wept with fear.
As Hades offered me his outstretched hand,
I flinched from him and clenched my trembling fists.

He bade me then to take his hand's contents,
A small red fruit with tiny ruby seeds.
The god of many names, his countenance kind,
Pressed each small icy seed into my palm.

'Persephone, I'll never do you harm.
For years I've loved and watched you from afar.
Become my wife and you shall be the queen
Of everything that lives and moves about.

But if you wish to flee from me right now,
I'll trouble you no more and leave you be.
I brought you down here not to be your jailer,
But to show you the lands you might yet rule.'

Three days and nights I spent in Hades' world.
I grew to know his kingdom as my own.
When that third night fell on the river Styx,
I knew that I had made my final choice.

'I shall take these three seeds and be your bride,
If only you will grant me one small thing.
I wish to plant these seeds in darkness here,
And turn your endless winter into spring.'

So maidens, when you find you are now crones,
And when your kindest days all seem long past,
When winter sinks into your tired bones,
Prepare yourself to meet me then at last.

I'll guide you down the long unending halls
And bear you gently to the low beyond,
Where you will dine beside the ones you've lost
And join us in an everlasting bond.

听我说，游历荒野的少女们，
你们的双眼尚未见过死亡，
常在日光渐暗时迟迟不归，
久久徘徊于石冢与幽暗洞穴旁。

我的心与灵魂也曾和你们一样。
我是珀耳塞福涅，被掳走的女子。
年轻时，我独自播下种子，
在阳光下自在地采集鲜花。

有一天，大地猛然裂开，
灰烬恶狠狠地喷涌，洒落大地。
冥王哈迪斯，死亡之主，为我而来，
要将我夺去，强娶为妻。

起初，我向地上的世界呼喊，
却无人听见，无人伸手拉住我。
他把我拉入地下的彼岸，
我知道，这里将是我的墓地。

死亡的世界里没有鲜花生长。
我倒在地上，恐惧地哭泣。
哈迪斯向我伸出手时，
我畏缩着躲开，攥紧颤抖的双拳。

随后，他让我接过掌中之物，
一颗红色的小果实，籽如细小的红宝石。
这位有着诸多名号的神，面容和善，
把一粒粒冰凉的种子放进我掌心。

“珀耳塞福涅，我绝不会伤害你。
多年来，我一直爱着你，从远处望着你。
做我的妻子，你便会成为女王，
统领一切活着、行走着的生灵。

但若你现在就想离我而去，
我便不再纠缠，任你离开。
我带你下来，并非要做你的狱卒，
而是让你看看将来或可统治的土地。”

我在哈迪斯的世界度过三天三夜。
渐渐熟悉他的王国，仿佛那是我的家园。
当第三个夜晚降临冥河斯堤克斯，
我知道，我已作出最后的选择。

“我愿收下这三粒种子，成为你的新娘，
只求你答应我一件小事。
我想把这些种子种在此处的黑暗里，
将你无尽的寒冬化作春天。”

所以，少女们，当你们也成了老妇，
当最美好的日子都仿佛远去，
当寒冬渗入你们疲惫的骨头，
就准备好，终于来与我相见吧。

我会引你们走过漫长无尽的厅堂，
轻柔地将你们带往地下彼岸，
在那里，你们将与逝去的亲人朋友同席，
与我们结下永恒的羁绊。

The Queen is one of the kindest people I've ever met, and her people love her dearly. Gertrude isn't Danish, but married into the throne via her late husband, the King Hamlet. As is traditional, she remarried to the King's brother after his death—now she is Claudius's wife.

After my mother passed away when I was a child, Gertrude took Laertes and me under her wing. I've been eternally grateful to her for her kindness ever since.

Gertrude was born in Austria, and is a member of the illustrious Hapsburg family. In fact, her father is the Emperor Maximilian I. She's worked incredibly hard to learn Danish and eliminate her accent. I know she has a sister as well, who lives outside Denmark. Royal blood runs thick through her veins.

Irma is one of the most feared women in Elsinore for her quick temper. She's fiercely devoted to the Queen, and originally followed Gertrude from Bohemia, where she and Gertrude were both born and raised.

Despite her teeth, I've seen that she has a warm side. She loves to gamble, and she's quite good; I wouldn't make a bet against her for all the world.

And there's a possibility... that what happened here might help me, somehow, in the future.

entries.source: Guildenstern and Hamlet came to a confrontation when we were all on the ship together. It's still hard to make sense of it all, but she pointed out to Hamlet that he has a history of chasing women who represent some kind of exotic 'other' to him. Women like Guildenstern. Women like me.
